title: DMA & Interrupt-Driven I/O
summary: Polling, interrupts, and DMA as three points on a spectrum trading CPU involvement for latency and complexity.

slides.markdown:
**Polling** is the simplest way for a CPU to talk to a device: it repeatedly checks a status register in a loop — "is the data ready yet? ...is it ready yet?" — until the device signals it's done.

It's trivial to implement and has essentially zero response latency once the device is actually ready, since the CPU notices the instant it checks. The cost is equally obvious: the CPU is **spinning, doing nothing else**, for however long the device takes — a wasteful trade whenever that wait is longer than a few cycles.

**Interrupt-driven I/O** flips the arrangement: instead of the CPU asking repeatedly, the device raises an **interrupt** — a hardware signal that pauses whatever the CPU is doing and jumps it to a handler — only when it's actually ready.

Between issuing the request and the interrupt firing, the CPU is completely free to do other work — run other processes, handle other I/O. This is why interrupts are the default model for most I/O today: they let one CPU juggle far more concurrent devices than polling ever could, since it's never stuck waiting on any single one.

**DMA (Direct Memory Access)** removes the CPU from the data path entirely for bulk transfers. The CPU sets up a **DMA controller** — telling it source, destination, and length — then goes back to other work; the DMA controller moves the actual bytes between the device and memory on its own, without the CPU touching each byte.

Only when the *entire* transfer finishes does the DMA controller raise an interrupt to tell the CPU it's done. This matters enormously for large transfers (a disk read, a network packet burst) — without DMA, the CPU would have to shuttle every single byte itself, wasting cycles that scale with data size instead of just with the number of requests.

Sequencing the steps shows exactly where the CPU is and isn't involved: it sets up the transfer, disappears, and only reappears when notified.

![A DMA transfer sequence: CPU configures the DMA controller, the controller moves data directly between device and memory, then an interrupt signals completion](assets/dma-transfer-sequence.svg)

The CPU's total involvement is two short steps — setup and handling the completion interrupt — regardless of whether the transfer moves a kilobyte or a gigabyte; the bulk data movement itself never touches CPU cycles at all.

slides.markdown:
The three approaches trade CPU cycles, latency, and implementation complexity against each other differently.

| | Polling | Interrupts | DMA |
|---|---|---|---|
| CPU cycles spent | High (busy-waits) | Low (only handles the interrupt) | Lowest (skips per-byte involvement) |
| Latency to notice "ready" | Immediate | Small overhead (context switch to handler) | Same as interrupts, plus transfer time |
| Implementation complexity | Simplest | Moderate (handler, priorities) | Highest (controller setup, buffer/coherency management) |

Modern systems typically layer all three: interrupts (or polling, situationally) signal *readiness*, and DMA handles the *bulk data movement* once a transfer is underway.

It's tempting to assume interrupts always beat polling — after all, they free the CPU. But every interrupt carries **fixed overhead**: saving/restoring CPU state, jumping to a handler, jumping back. For a device generating requests at **very high frequency** — a fast NIC receiving packets at line rate, for example — that fixed cost paid on *every single event* can add up to more total overhead than just polling would.

This is why some high-performance network drivers switch to polling (or a hybrid — interrupts at low load, polling under sustained high load) specifically to avoid interrupt storms overwhelming the CPU with handler overhead. The right choice depends on event frequency, not a universal rule that interrupts are always better.
